title: Map the work before buying another tool
content:
New tools are easy to demonstrate. The work they need to improve is harder to understand.

Describe the real trigger

Begin with what actually starts the work: an email, a customer enquiry, a completed job, a new employee or the end of a reporting period. Avoid beginning with a proposed tool.

Follow the information

Where is the information first recorded? Who touches it next? Where does it need to be visible? Mark every copy, wait, rekey and decision. This creates a shared view of the work instead of a collection of personal workarounds.

Name the roles

For each step, label the role: system of record, repeatable automation, AI assistance or human judgement. If a step has no clear role, it is a useful question—not something to hide.

Test the better version

Show how a routine case moves, then show an exception. A believable workflow explains what happens when information is missing or a person says no.

Use the lab as a starting point

Choose the closest workflow example, compare the old way with the better way, and use the pattern to start a conversation about your own process. The result is illustrative—not a substitute for understanding your business.

title: Sometimes the answer is: do not automate this
content:
Not every manual step is waste. Some are checks, relationships or decisions that deserve attention.

Do not automate a process that changes every week

When the rule is still being negotiated, stabilise the process first. Otherwise each change becomes another fragile exception hidden inside a workflow.

Do not automate unclear ownership

If nobody agrees who owns the next action, software will only move the uncertainty faster. Decide the owner, the escalation path and the definition of complete.

Do not use AI where a simple rule is enough

A fixed approval threshold, a standard reminder or a known routing rule does not need a probabilistic model. Deterministic automation is easier to test, explain and maintain.

Check what existing software can do

Before adding a connector or agent, look for a native setting, report, notification or field that solves the practical problem. Fewer moving parts can be the better outcome.

Choose a smaller first win

Start with a bounded process that repeats often, has a clear owner and can be measured. Make exceptions visible. Then decide whether the next improvement is worth it. Explore the job-to-invoice workflow

title: Lead routing: what should happen in the first 15 minutes?
content:
Leads are often missed in the gap between “someone enquired” and “someone owns the next step.”

Make ownership immediate

An enquiry needs a clear destination, a named owner and a visible next action. A shared mailbox is rarely a reliable workflow by itself; it is a place where a workflow might start.

Use rules before intelligence

Known location, service type, customer status or availability can often assign work predictably. If an enquiry is unstructured, AI may help identify a category or draft a summary—then a person can confirm the important details.

Keep the customer experience human

An acknowledgement can set expectations, but it should not pretend a complex request has been understood or promise a result. The best follow-up feels timely, specific and accountable.

Measure the right gap

Track time to first owned action, not just time to send an automatic reply. Also review unassigned enquiries, reassignment loops and outcomes by source.

Explore the visual pattern

The lead-routing example makes the handoff visible: capture, qualify, assign, notify and follow up, with a person still able to intervene.

title: Human approval is a feature, not a failure
content:
The point of a better workflow is not to remove people. It is to remove avoidable effort and make important decisions clearer.

Keep people where judgement matters

Approval is valuable when the amount is unusual, the customer relationship is sensitive, the information is incomplete or the decision has a real consequence. Make the review point visible, timely and informed.

Do not make people check everything

Routine cases can move with rules. A good workflow highlights the small number of cases that need attention: missing documents, mismatched values, unclear requests or an exception to policy. This protects judgement from being buried under administration.

Give the reviewer context

A useful approval asks one clear question and shows the source, relevant history and recommended next step. It should not force someone to open five systems just to understand what they are approving.

Design an exit path

Every automated action needs a way to pause, correct and continue. A visible exception queue and clear owner are more trustworthy than an opaque “set and forget” process.

See approval in a job-to-invoice example

The invoice workflow lets a person review unapproved variations before an invoice draft is prepared. This fictional demonstration does not send an invoice or make a payment.

title: Your systems do not need replacing to work together
content:
A business can own good software and still have a difficult process. The gap is often what happens between the tools: email handovers, spreadsheet workarounds, duplicated records and missing status updates.

Start with a moment of friction

Choose a real sentence your team says: “Finance does not know the job is complete,” “we wait for that mailbox,” or “the sales team never updates the CRM.” That is a better design brief than a list of software features.

Find the source, destination and decision

For that moment, identify where information begins, where it must be visible next, and who should decide when something is not normal. A connection is only useful when those responsibilities are clear.

Connect deliberately

Some systems have native features that already solve the problem. Some need a simple integration. Some need an intermediary workflow with a log, alerts and an exception queue. Buying a new platform is only one option—and often not the first one.

Make the change understandable

Show the old path beside the better path. Include the manual handoffs removed, the information still verified by people, and what happens if a connection fails.

Explore a familiar example

The lead-routing workflow shows a common pattern: capture, assign, notify and follow up—without treating the CRM as a decorative destination.

title: Automation or AI: which job does this process need?
content:
“Use AI” is not a process design. A better question is: what kind of work is this step actually asking for?

System: keep the record true

Your accounting, job, CRM or HR system is usually where the official transaction or status belongs. It should remain the source of truth.

Automation: move repeatable work

Automation is useful when the rule is clear: notify a person, create a task, copy an approved field, schedule a follow-up or route a known category. It should be observable and easy to recover when a connected service changes.

AI: help with interpretation

AI can classify a free-text enquiry, summarise a long document, draft a response or identify information that needs review. It is probabilistic. Give it a narrow task, clear guardrails and a visible confidence or review point.

Human: retain judgement

People should own approvals, customer relationships, unusual cases, accountability and decisions with meaningful consequences. Human review is not a failure of automation; it is good design.

Try the framework in context

In the customer-enquiry example, an illustrative AI step helps understand an enquiry, while a person remains responsible for the answer and next action.

A useful test

If a step cannot explain what happens when it is wrong, it is not ready to be automated. Start with a smaller, observable version instead.

title: Which number is right? A reporting handover checklist
content:
Before choosing a new dashboard, ask two people to explain the same number. If they give different sources, periods or definitions, the first job is to agree the handover.

Try this with one report

Choose a figure people question in a regular meeting. It might be open enquiries, completed work, available capacity or invoiced revenue. This is a working checklist, not a claim about your reporting time or data quality.

  1. Definition: What does the number include and exclude? Write the unit and the decision it supports.
  2. Period and cut-off: Which dates are included, in which time zone, and when do adjustments stop?
  3. Source and owner: Which record is authoritative? Who can explain a correction?
  4. Freshness: When was each source refreshed? Show missing or stale extracts instead of treating them as zero.
  5. Reconciliation: Which references and totals must agree? Keep a difference separate until it has been resolved.
  6. Exception: Who owns an unresolved difference, when is it reviewed and what can the team decide while it remains open?

A fictional handover

One team counts completed jobs. Another counts invoices issued. Those are different measures, even if both are called “finished work”. Agree the labels before connecting the sources. A daily refresh cannot repair an undefined number.

See a report held for review

The daily reporting story explains how Excel, Xero and Simpro records are matched and reconciled. An unresolved record is held for review and rerun. The demonstration uses fictional records, not business results.

Bring a useful starting point

Write down the report, the disputed measure, its sources and the person who owns the next decision. Do not include private records when experimenting with an AI tool.

title: Why are we entering this twice?
content:
Duplicate entry is not a people problem. It is usually a handover problem.

A job is created in one system, copied into a spreadsheet, then typed into finance software. Each person is trying to keep the business moving. The work is real; the retyping is often unnecessary.

Start with one piece of information

Pick something that gets entered repeatedly: a customer name, job number, invoice amount, new-starter details or a lead. Write down where it starts, who copies it, and where it must end up. This reveals the process between the software—not just the software itself.

Ask four useful questions

  1. Which system should own the record?
  2. Is the next step a repeatable rule or a judgement call?
  3. What must be checked before it moves?
  4. What happens when the information is missing or unusual?

If a step is repeatable, automation can carry it. If information needs interpreting, AI may assist with a draft or classification. If the consequence matters, a person should approve the exception.

Do not automate a bad handover

Connecting two messy processes can make errors move faster. First agree on the source of truth, the minimum information required and the visible exception path. Then connect the routine work.

See the pattern

Explore the job-to-invoice workflow to see an illustrative example: the system moves known information, an automation applies consistent steps, and a person keeps review and sending decisions.

A better first measure

Count duplicate entries and waiting points for one week. That gives you a credible starting point—without pretending every improvement can be reduced to a dollar figure.
